item.title: Palau Visitors Authority reports 76% tourism recovery from pre-pandemic levels
item.description: Palau Visitors Authority is reporting a 76% recovery in visitor arrivals compared with pre-pandemic levels. There were 71,681 visitors last year, compared with 93,723 in 2019.
item.content:encoded:
Palau Visitors Authority is reporting a 76% recovery in visitor arrivals compared with pre-pandemic levels.

There were 71,681 visitors last year, compared with 93,723 in 2019.

As of September, 63,948 people had traveled to Palau, meaning the country is on track to exceed last year’s total arrivals.

The Visitors Authority says that in 2025, Palau recorded the highest number of American, Australian and European tourists in the nation’s history. China remained Palau’s top visitor source market, with Taiwan ranking second.

The average visitor stay in Palau was a record 5.9 nights in 2025.

item.title: PBS Guam to host annual pledge drive Saturday
item.description: PBS Guam will host its annual Pledge Drive, “The Story Continues,” on Saturday. The broadcast will feature local performances, previews of upcoming local programs, and updates on returning shows.
item.content:encoded:
PBS Guam will host its annual Pledge Drive, “The Story Continues,” on Saturday.

The broadcast will feature local performances, previews of upcoming local programs, and updates on returning shows.

The annual fundraiser supports PBS Guam’s educational, cultural, and locally produced programming. The station relies on contributions from viewers, government, and foundations to continue providing educational content and sharing Guam’s stories.

PBS Guam is offering pledge gifts based on donation amounts. Donors who contribute $75 will receive a PBS Guam merchandise mystery box. A $100 donation includes a windbreaker, tote bag, director’s hat, and one year of PBS Passport access. A $150 donation includes all four gifts and one year of PBS Passport access, which provides an on-demand library of PBS programs, shows, and documentaries.

The pledge drive will air on KGTF Channel 12 and stream through the PBS App and YouTube at youtube.com/pbsguam . Rebroadcasts will air on KGTF Channel 12 every Sunday evening throughout Nov.

Community members can donate online at pbsguam.org/support or call 671-734-5483 for more information.

item.title: Regulators greenlight landmark solar project for CNMI
item.description: After weeks of public hearings, scrutiny and debate, CNMI regulators on Thursday approved a landmark solar power project that officials say could reduce the commonwealth's dependence on imported fuel and bring long-term savings to utility customers. The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission voted unanimously to approve the power purchase agreement and related contracts between the Commonwealth
item.content:encoded:
After weeks of public hearings, scrutiny and debate, CNMI regulators on Thursday approved a landmark solar power project that officials say could reduce the commonwealth's dependence on imported fuel and bring long-term savings to utility customers.

The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission voted unanimously to approve the power purchase agreement and related contracts between the Commonwealth Utilities Corp. and developer Eastern Power Solutions, clearing a major hurdle for the proposed $500 million renewable energy initiative.

The project would establish a utility-scale solar and battery energy storage system for CUC and has drawn significant public attention amid concerns over its costs, financing structure and long-term impact on ratepayers.

The vote came just two days before an Oct. 31 deadline set by Eastern Power Solutions, which previously warned regulators it would withdraw its proposal if a decision was not reached. The company said the deadline was tied to financing requirements and a Dec. 31, 2027, federal tax-credit deadline critical to the project's economic viability.

Acting Chair Bruce Camacho and Commissioner Jack Angelo voted in person, while Commissioner James Mendiola participated virtually from Tinian.

"We've had a great turnout. We've had a lot of great public input," Mendiola said before the vote. He said commissioners had spent countless hours reviewing the extensive legal and financial documentation supporting the project.

"There are no easy decisions for the CNMI," Mendiola said. "There's an element of risk on both sides, and we have to weigh the risk."

Camacho said commissioners thoroughly reviewed the proposal despite concerns raised in public testimony and written comments.

"I think we've done everything on our side to properly review this proposal," he said.

Angelo rejected suggestions that the commission was responsible for delays, noting regulators identified issues involving land documentation and liability protections that required correction before approval.

"Our goal was to protect the ratepayers, but also regulate and oversee the utilities," Angelo said.

CPUC legal counsel James Sirok said concerns raised during the review process were adequately addressed and that nothing remained that should prevent commissioners from voting on the proposal.

Following the vote, CUC Executive Director Kevin Watson said the project represents a significant step toward modernizing the commonwealth's power system.

"We're on the way to making improvements within the utilities and CNMI, and these improvements will help our customers bring us forward with renewable power," Watson told reporters.

Watson said electricity generated under the agreement is expected to cost about 18.5 cents per kilowatt-hour for 25 years without escalation, compared with roughly 44 cents per kilowatt-hour today.

While immediate savings are not expected, Watson said lower fuel costs could begin benefiting customers once construction is completed and the solar facilities begin generating power, likely in 2028.

The primary solar facility is planned for the Naftan area near Saipan International Airport. Watson said CUC hopes to break ground soon and celebrate the project's launch with the community in the coming weeks.

item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration is still detaining pregnant migrant youth in a region of Texas where a lack of specialized obstetric care can be life threatening for them, an investigation by The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom has found. The practice continues despite vocal concern from current and former government officials, and from members of Congress.

Government records show that in the first ten months of the policy, four of the 21 pregnant girls placed in the region had to be transferred out of state to receive specialized medical care, including at least one abortion, that is unavailable in Texas.

"The first time that happened should have been a wake-up call for the administration, and they should have stopped placing kids in any remote area where they can't get care," said Jen Smyers, who during the Biden administration helped oversee the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), which is responsible for migrant youth who are apprehended by immigration authorities without a parent or guardian.

She called the policy to send all pregnant children to South Texas "enraging."

This spring, The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom published a joint investigation revealing the administration's policy of detaining pregnant unaccompanied minors as young as 13, at least half of whom were pregnant as a result of rape, at a single shelter in the city of San Benito near Texas' border with Mexico. The investigation detailed serious concerns that health experts inside and outside the government had raised about the policy, given that adolescent pregnancies are inherently high risk and there is a lack of specialized obstetric care in the region.

Since then, the administration has denied that there is such a policy and said it is ensuring that the girls have access to the care they need.

In an email in September the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees ORR, wrote that "ORR's policies for placing children in its custody into care provider facilities are based on child welfare best practices in order to provide a safe environment and place the child in the least restrictive setting appropriate for the child's needs. This is especially true for expectant minors in ORR care."

Yet the administration's own records, as well as interviews with multiple government officials, suggest otherwise.

The documents, which were obtained through a public records request, show that ORR explicitly directed its staff in July 2025 to send all pregnant youth to the shelter in San Benito, just outside Brownsville at the extreme southern tip of Texas.

Several months later, internal agency data showed that pregnant girls started being sent to a different shelter nearby instead, according to three ORR officials who asked not to be named because they feared retaliation.

Forty-eight Democratic members of Congress demanded transparency about the policy in a pointed letter to the Department of Health and Human Services back in April. They received a response in September from an assistant secretary at HHS, Alex J. Adams, who wrote that ORR "does not make placement decisions for pregnant youth based on a blanket rule or one-size-fits-all approach" and that it "takes seriously its responsibility to protect the health, safety, dignity, and well-being of every unaccompanied alien child in its custody."

HHS did not respond to requests for comment about the discrepancy between the statements in Adams' letter and the government's own records.

"Obviously, they're not being honest about their policy," said U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, a Democrat from San Antonio, whose office authored the letter to HHS.

"It's irresponsible that they would wait several months to respond to basic questions about the care of some of the most vulnerable people within the system," Castro said, adding that the administration failed to explain "what seems to be an informal but strict policy of sending these girls to deep South Texas, which lacks the medical care that the girls need."

Unaccompanied migrant children have historically been placed in shelters across the United States, but this summer, the Trump administration began detaining far more of them in Texas . According to internal reports provided independently by two of the ORR officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity, 95% of the roughly 300 children apprehended by immigration officials in September were placed in detention in Texas, up from 45% in June.

Advocates for unaccompanied migrant children, former government officials, and some members of Congress have criticized the move, arguing that the state is not prepared to handle an influx of vulnerable children, some of whom need special care.

The fact that ORR has had to transfer several pregnant unaccompanied minors out of Texas to receive medical care, one congress member says, proves their point.

"If the government had to fly or transport these pregnant children across the country to get them the medical care they need, why on earth did it deliberately send them to Texas in the first place?" said U.S. Rep. Judy Chu, a Democrat from Southern California who signed the congressional inquiry letter to HHS.

"If there is a 13-year-old girl who has survived rape," she said, "she should be met with compassion, safety and appropriate medical care. Instead, this administration is placing children like her in a state where they will be deprived of access to basic healthcare. It's dangerous, and it's cruel, and there's no excuse for treating children this way."

Government records contradict Trump administration's claims

Unlike Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which detains migrant adults and families in large, prison-like facilities, ORR holds unaccompanied children in group or foster homes overseen by private contractors. Laws, agency regulations and court orders require that the children receive comprehensive healthcare and appropriate education while they're detained.

In an emailed statement last month, HHS said that placing children in Texas is "operationally efficient" and that ORR's facilities in the state "provide all requirements and more." But records obtained through a public information request cast doubt on that assertion.

The records show between July of 2025, when ORR began placing pregnant girls in South Texas, and May of 2026, four of them had to be transferred to other states to receive medical treatment.

That's roughly one in five of the 21 pregnant girls the agency placed in the region in that time frame, according to one of the ORR officials who requested anonymity.

In detailed notes for one of those cases, ORR staff wrote that a pregnant 12-year-old girl was transferred from the Rio Grande Valley to a shelter in New York on the recommendation of ORR's division of health. The records note that the child needed access to specialists whose availability in South Texas is "extremely limited."

In a note for another case, staff wrote that a pregnant girl was transferred to California due to an unspecified "high risk medical need." In at least one case, a girl was transferred out of Texas because she had requested an abortion, the records show.

Marsha Griffin, a retired professor of pediatrics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley School of Medicine, said such outcomes were inevitable. Griffin said the shelters have very few medical staff on hand and the region does not have enough specialized obstetricians.

"Young girls who are pregnant, especially those from 10 to 14 years of age, are automatically a high-risk population," said Griffin, who oversaw medical students volunteering in ORR facilities in South Texas.

Internal communications, also obtained through a public records request, show that officials in ORR's own division of health warned the agency's leadership about the lack of pregnancy-related healthcare in the Rio Grande Valley.

"Texas has one of the worst rates of maternal mortality in the U.S.," wrote Joanna Gaines, who at the time was ORR's acting health director, in a July 18, 2025, email to Melissa Johnston, the agency's head of operations. She added that the state "lack[s] access to quality perinatal healthcare" and that the Rio Grande Valley's Cameron County "has one of the higher rates of infant mortality in Texas."

item.title: Halloween temperatures have been trending hotter. Here's what the data shows
item.description: Halloween is getting hotter. Researchers from the educational nonprofit Climate Central analyzed fall temperatures across the United States. They found that, on average, autumn temperatures have increased by nearly three degrees Fahrenheit since the 1970s. From member station Houston Public Media, Natalie Weber tells us more about what their findings mean for trick-or-treaters across the country.
item.content:encoded:
Halloween is getting hotter. Researchers from the educational nonprofit Climate Central analyzed fall temperatures across the United States. They found that, on average, autumn temperatures have increased by nearly three degrees Fahrenheit since the 1970s. From member station Houston Public Media, Natalie Weber tells us more about what their findings mean for trick-or-treaters across the country.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: Whoa. We got a princess and a dinosaur. All right (laughter).

NATALIE WEBER, BYLINE: On a warm Friday afternoon in early October, Eduardo and Mary Reyes are at a pumpkin patch with their two kids, 7-year-old Leonardo and 3-year-old Lorelei.

WEBER: While other kids have opted for shorts and T-shirts in the nearly 90-degree weather, Lorelei is dressed as Elsa from the movie "Frozen," and Leonardo is in a velociraptor costume.

How are you feeling, like, temperature wise? Are you hot, or are you just right?

WEBER: Mary Reyes grew up in Houston, so she didn't always have to wear a jacket when she dressed up for Halloween as a kid.

MARY REYES: I want to say if it was a costume with a long sleeve, we would be OK. If not, maybe, like, a little light jacket, a sweater.

REYES: Definitely no sweaters. We do try to shy away from the costumes that have the long sleeve. We just hope it's not too hot on Halloween Day.

WEBER: Reyes' experience reflects a pattern in the nation's weather. Fall temperatures have been getting hotter across the U.S. as summer-like weather lasts longer than it did about 50 years ago. Climate Central chief meteorologist Shel Winkley says in the northern U.S., summer temperatures are persisting through September. But in the South, this warmer weather can last into October.

To measure this, researchers at Climate Central look at wind cities are seeing their last day of warm temperatures. For example, in Atlanta, they look at the last day of weather above 85 degrees Fahrenheit. For Anchorage, Alaska, researchers analyze the final day of temperatures above 60 degrees.

Winkley lives in Texas. Last year, he carved pumpkins with his kids on the weekend before Halloween.

SHEL WINKLEY: And it was so hot that before we actually got to Halloween day, the pumpkins were already rotted and, like, falling apart and shriveled because it was so hot outside.

WEBER: Bernadette Woods Placky is a meteorologist and executive director at the Talking Climate Collaborative, a new nonprofit organization focused on climate change. She says human-caused climate change is the leading cause of warming fall temperatures. But this year, the hotter weather is being exacerbated by El Nino. That's a naturally occurring climate pattern that happens every two to seven years and increases global temperatures.

BERNADETTE WOODS PLACKY: This year, we're seeing spikes in some areas on top of that overall warming because of El Nino and this being such a strong, record-breaking El Nino, giving that extra push of temperatures in our atmosphere.

WEBER: At the pumpkin patch outside of Houston, Reyes says her family is looking forward to some relief from the summer temperatures.

REYES: We're really excited for Halloween, as we are every year, especially kind of getting over that, like, heat of the summer. We're looking forward to that fall weather. It's not always here during the month of October, but we're always hoping.

WEBER: For now, they're not letting the weather get in the way of enjoying their Halloween costumes. For NPR News, I'm Natalie Weber in Houston. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.title: Here's what it's like to live in Salem, Mass., during the Halloween tourism season
item.description: It is a pretty good time to be a witch in Salem, Massachusetts, certainly compared to 1692, when dozens of witchcraft claims led to 19 public executions plus other deaths in prison. item.content:encoded:
It is a pretty good time to be a witch in Salem, Massachusetts, certainly compared to 1692, when dozens of witchcraft claims led to 19 public executions plus other deaths in prison. This was, of course, the Salem witch trials. Over 300 years later, the story is why a different of mass hysteria takes over Salem every fall. The small city just north of Boston has become enormously popular for Halloween tourists in October. Reporter Megan Johnson has written about what that is like for boston.com and is with us now. Welcome.

DETROW: Tell me what the draw is. I mean, it makes sense. This historic town tied to witch trials - makes sense that it would be a Halloween destination. But, like, what is there to do? Say you're thinking of driving up to Salem to check it out in October. What's available?

JOHNSON: There is so much to do. Besides the fact that it is just an absolutely stunning town that is the epitome of autumn when the weather changes, people love the historic aspect, so they want to go to the Salem Witch Museum, the House of Seven Gables, the nun on stilts, which is one of the very common buskers on the street. There's people in costume all the time. It's a big bachelorette trip draw.

DETROW: Has all of this grown in recent years? Like, and is there...

DETROW: ...A particular reason for that?

JOHNSON: So it has grown tremendously in recent years, pretty across the board, every resident has said. And a lot of them really attribute that to social media - Instagram, social media influencers who descend upon the city and want to caption amazing content. And because there's so much of that content out there, that brings such a draw of visitors who see it and want to participate in it, too.

DETROW: So let's set the scene. It's about 45,000 people live in Salem, and - what? - a million people visit in October. What is that like on a fall Saturday?

JOHNSON: The No. 1 complaint that people have is that it's nonstop traffic, and there's nowhere to park, and that comes from residents and visitors. But there's also just a constant onslaught of people in the streets, which often get shut down as an attempt to get rid of some of the traffic. But moving around, navigating the streets is pretty crazy.

DETROW: You wrote about a bunch of different examples of funny run-ins between residents and Halloween tourists. Can you tell us a couple of them?

JOHNSON: Yes. They really range from the overwhelmingly positive - people who have met just wonderful people, like the World Cup visitors from Scotland. They just thought they were absolutely wonderful. But then the people who have visitors throwing bottles in their yards, busting up their pumpkins, nonstop tours walking through their streets maybe three times an hour. And the kind of most unusual thing is that a lot of tourists don't seem to realize that there are actual residents who are living there. So it kind of Disney-fies the experience for many of them. They just see it as kind of a play town when really there's people behind those doors that they're accidentally walking into.

DETROW: What is your best suggestion for somebody who, on one hand, says, this sounds great, and on the other hand, says, I don't want to make it worse for these poor people who live in Salem? Like, how can you enjoy the experience without being that person?

JOHNSON: They really want to encourage whatever people can do to not drive into the city. Because there's so little parking for residents already, there's already so little parking for visitors, as well. The Salem commuter rail on the MBTA is very already very filled, so a lot of people are on there. But one of the best recommendations that I got from a city counselor was, take an Uber, have it drop you off on the outskirts of the city, and you can walk in and not have to worry about anything, including the high price of parking.

DETROW: Megan Johnson - her story about spooky season in Salem, Massachusetts, is on boston.com. Thank you so much.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.title: Judge orders an inquiry into potential DOJ misconduct in Trump's golf course case

item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — A federal judge is launching a formal inquiry into potential misconduct by Trump administration officials in the lawsuit over East Potomac Park, including whether they repeatedly misrepresented the president's plans for the municipal D.C. golf course.

District Judge Ana Reyes ordered Friday's hearing — the third in as many weeks — to seek clarity from government lawyers days after they acknowledged in writing Wednesday that there is a plan to transform the municipal golf course into a championship-level venue, closing it and much of the surrounding park in mid-November.

For months, Justice Department attorneys representing the Interior Department and National Park Service had maintained in court filings and hearings that such a plan was not yet final, despite President Trump's social media statements proclaiming otherwise.

Their abrupt confirmation on Wednesday night prompted Reyes to call both sides back into court, just days after she ordered a halt to tree-clearing and major renovations at the park (which the government promptly appealed).

Reyes opened Friday's hearing by quoting the D.C. Bar Rule of Professional Conduct 3.3 , which prohibits lawyers from knowingly making or failing to correct false statements to the court. She asked Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr., who is leading the government's defense, whether there was anything he would like to correct.

"Not to my knowledge," Woodward said, explaining that he hasn't read every transcript in the case. "We have lots of binders," he said, to which Reyes replied: "I bet you do."

Over the next four hours, Reyes grilled Woodward about the timing and status of the administration's renovation plans. She demanded to know whether officials had not been truthful when they told her last Monday that they were not aware of the park closure that Trump had posted about that same morning.

Reyes called the lawyers' claims into doubt for two main reasons.

Government lawyers acknowledged for the first time in their Wednesday filing that the administration is closing the park next month, both for golf course renovations and to address the man-made peninsula's crumbling seawall. And they said in court that they submitted those renovation plans to the National Capital Planning Commission for review on Friday.

Under questioning, Woodward told the judge that the submission had been in the works for several weeks. But, as Reyes fired back incredulously, no one from the government mentioned that in the previous hearings, one of which lasted seven hours.

"Am I to understand that for weeks someone has been putting pen to paper on a submission to design the golf course … while this litigation was ongoing, while Department of Justice employees were representing to me that there was no plan?" she said.

The hearing ended with Reyes announcing that she would "open a formal inquiry into whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and [Justice Department] attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated applicable ethical rules."

Reyes said that inquiry may be led by a special master, whom she has not yet appointed but described as a judicial officer with "full investigatory powers." Reyes said if the government rejects her special master, she will conduct the inquiry herself.

Reyes stressed that the opening of an investigation does not mean that the court has found or will find evidence that any government lawyers have violated their professional obligations.

But the relatively unusual move suggests that the judge is finished taking the administration at its word, as she said she has done since local historic preservation advocates and golfers first filed suit in February.

The legal fight kicked into high gear earlier this month when the Trump administration cut down hundreds of trees with less than a day's notice. Officials have denied that the tree-clearing was part of a broader plan to renovate the golf course, but Reyes called it a pretext for beginning work without proper approvals. On Friday, she also ordered the government officials to preserve all relevant documents so the "court can conduct an inquiry without the loss of evidence."

"Trial lawyers sometimes tell juries, 'Trust but verify,'" Reyes said from the bench on Friday. "For months, the court trusted, but did not verify. No longer."

On Monday, Reyes extended her ban on further tree removal and required the government to provide 10 days' written notice before closing or irreversibly modifying East Potomac, which the administration quickly appealed.

She issued a blistering 70-page opinion in which she said the case had become about much more than golf.

"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president," Reyes wrote.

Within hours of Reyes' ruling, Trump took to social media to double down on his plan to start renovations in November, saying Reyes "has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project."

In response, Reyes scheduled Friday's hearing and ordered the government — including Woodward specifically — to "come prepared to state" whether it continues to maintain that there is no final plan, among other details.

But the reply came even sooner, in a Justice Department filing Wednesday night.

Government lawyers said the National Park Service would submit a plan Friday to the National Capital Planning Commission to review "a rendering designed by Tom Fazio for a World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events."

And they said they would soon "close East Potomac Park south of Buckeye Drive, including the Golf Course, consistent with the President's directive."

The filing says the National Park Service entered into a new lease agreement with the National Links Trust — the nonprofit that operates the golf course — on Wednesday.

Under that new agreement, which was confirmed by the National Links Trust, the organization will continue to operate D.C.'s other two municipal golf courses under a 50-year lease, but cease operations at East Potomac "as of close of business on or before November 15."

But details of that plan were still hazy in the courtroom on Friday. Reyes spent most of the hearing questioning Woodward, the third-highest-ranking official at the Justice Department.

At one point, Reyes accused Woodward of "playing games with words" at last week's hearing and said she refused to do so again. Later, when Woodward characterized Trump's Truth Social announcements as a matter of executive privilege, Reyes erupted: "He posted it!"

One particularly protracted back-and-forth focused on whether Trump's Truth Social posts announcing the golf course's forthcoming closure constituted "plans."
